newsitem.title: CHINA: China bourse centralisation seen helping control.
newsitem.headline: China bourse centralisation seen helping control.

text.p: China's announcement on Friday that it has put the country's two stock exchanges under direct central government control would help boost supervision and development of the fledgling stock markets, analysts said.

The move would help China in its struggle to make its stock markets world class, with supervision and regulations to match, and cause foreign investors to feel more confident about putting money into the developing market, they said.
But it could also add more bureaucracy to the stock market industry and slow down decision making, the analysts added.
"The move will help strengthen supervision of the markets by effectively excluding local interests in stock trading," said one executive with a major Chinese brokerage.
The city governments of Shanghai and Shenzhen had recently seemed more interested in attracting business to their respective markets than following Beijing's rules, analysts said.

The State Council, China's cabinet, has ordered top securities watchdog the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), to take direct control of the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, state media said on Friday.
The move was expected to have little effect on the short term movement of share prices, especially foreign currency B shares which are rising on a wave of liquidity, brokers said.
"Rumours about a change in the management system of the stock exchanges have been circulating in the market for some time and have largely been digested," said one local analyst.
In another move, Tu Guangshao, formerly the head of the CSRC's transaction department, was named as the new president of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, replacing Yang Xianghai.
"Investors do not care much about who will be in charge of the stock exchanges," said another analyst.
Shanghai's B share index shrugged off the announcement to end the morning up 5.520 points, or 6.86 percent, to 86.016 points.
In Shenzhen, the B index rose 9.79 points, or 6.47 percent, to 161.01 points.
But domestic currency A shares reacted more cautiously.
The Shanghai A share index closed the morning down 10.643 points, or 0.87 percent, to 1,208.29 points. Shenzhen's A index lost 9.79 points, or 0.60 percent, to 379.72 points.

Domestic investors were perhaps more aware that the move reflected Beijing's deep disappointment with the exchanges and with local governments for failing to fully implement its policies, analysts said.
"The centralisation indicates the central government is disappointed with the local governments for being unable to implement its stock policies accurately," one analyst said.
Shoddy implementation of central government policies helped cause a market slump from mid-1994 to early 1996 and a stock fever that lasted from April last year to May this year, analysts said.
Beijing was forced to step in and rein in the markets in mid-May after share prices rose about 50 percent in the first four months of 1996, they said.
